title: Do Most New Businesses Really Fail in a Few Years?

scenes.direction: Title appears with s04, not before.
scenes.narration: You have probably heard some version of this at a party, on a podcast, or from a relative who wanted you to keep your day job. Most new businesses fail, and they fail fast.

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: Question types on, centred.
onScreenText: A measurement, or a slogan?

scenes.narration: It sounds like hard-won wisdom. But is it a measurement, or a slogan?

scenes.purpose: Introduce the BLS table as the instrument we will check against.

visual.description: The BLS survival table for the cohort opened in the year ended March 2015, rendered as a clean monospace table; the cohort header highlights, then the survival column softly glows row by row.

citations.label: BLS Business Employment Dynamics, establishment survival, openings in year ended March 2015

scenes.direction: Slow push-in on the table through s07.
scenes.narration: There is a way to check, because the US Bureau of Labor Statistics keeps a table that follows each year's newly opened private-sector establishments and counts how many are still operating, every year after they open. So let's put the slogan next to the table and see where they part ways.

scenes.purpose: Show the specific, multi-year version of the slogan.

visual.description: Quote card; the three figures (25%, 40%, half) brighten in turn as they are spoken.
onScreenText: "About 25% of businesses fail in their first year. 40% after 3 years, and half of businesses fail after 5 years."

scenes.narration: First, it helps to notice that the slogan comes in more than one size. Barry's Economics, a channel that pushes back on hustle podcasts, gives the most specific version: "About 25% of businesses fail in their first year. 40% after 3 years, and half of businesses fail after 5 years."

scenes.purpose: Contrast the two sizes of the slogan side by side.

visual.description: Two lines built one per sentence: the months version in amber, the years version in off-white beneath.
onScreenText: Gone before the season changes
Closer to a coin toss, spread over years

scenes.direction: Second line arrives on 'The other says'.
scenes.narration: Listen to how different that is from the first version. One says your shop is likely gone before the season changes. The other says starting a business is closer to a coin toss, spread over years.

scenes.purpose: The decade version, from a platform that sells online stores.

visual.description: Quote card in the same style as sc01; '34.7%' and 'a decade later' brighten.
onScreenText: "Only 34.7% of all US private-sector business establishments started in March 2013 were still operating a decade later."

citations.label: Shopify blog, Is Dropshipping Worth It

scenes.narration: And Shopify, the e-commerce platform, writes on its own blog that "Only 34.7% of all US private-sector business establishments started in March 2013 were still operating a decade later."

scenes.purpose: Frame the open question and set up following one cohort.

visual.description: The question types on; it stays through s14 and s15.
onScreenText: A few months, a few years, or a decade?

scenes.narration: So which is it: a few months, a few years, or a decade? And does any of it say something about an online store in particular, which is the business most of these videos are actually talking about? To answer that, we need one group of businesses, followed from the day they open.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the class of 2015 as one big number.

visual.description: One stat tile: 677,876 counts up as s16 is spoken, labelled as the new establishments of the year ended March 2015.

chart.title: New private-sector establishments, year ended March 2015

citations.label: BLS, establishment survival, openings in year ended March 2015

scenes.narration: In the year that ended in March 2015, 677,876 new private-sector establishments opened in the United States, according to the BLS table. Think of them as a class photo, retaken every March to see who is still in the picture.

scenes.purpose: The first year: a real loss, not most.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars: the full class at March 2015 and the 79.6% still operating at March 2016; the gap between them shades amber as s19 is spoken.

chart.title: Class of 2015, share still operating
chart.note: All new private-sector establishments, not online stores.

onScreenText: 20.4% closed within the first year

scenes.direction: Hold after 'But it is not most.'
scenes.narration: One year later, in March 2016, 539,701 of them were still operating: 79.6 percent of the class. Turn that around and 20.4 percent had closed within their first year. That is a real loss. But it is not most.

scenes.purpose: Three years in, and how much of the loss came in year one.

visual.description: The bars extend to March 2017 and March 2018; the year-one drop stays amber while the later drops are slate, so the first year visibly carries just over half the loss.
onScreenText: 20.4 of 38.6 points lost in year one

scenes.narration: By March 2018, three years in, 61.4 percent of the class was still open. So the first year accounts for a little over half of the closures in the first three years: 20.4 points of the 38.6 points lost.

scenes.purpose: Show that the yearly survival rate of survivors climbs: the danger is front-loaded.

visual.description: A new chart: each bar is the share of the previous March's survivors still operating a year later. The first three bars fill in as s23 names them; the March 2021 to March 2025 bars arrive together on s24.

chart.title: Share of last year's survivors still operating
chart.note: Each bar is a share of the previous year's survivors, not of the original class.

citations.label: BLS, establishment survival, class of 2015, survival since previous year

scenes.direction: Explicit wipe from sc12 so the viewer does not read these as the same measure.
scenes.narration: And the share of last year's survivors that make it through another year climbs, from 79.6 percent in the first year to 86.8 percent in the second and 88.9 percent in the third. From March 2021 on, it never drops below 92.4 percent. In other words, the danger is front-loaded. A business that makes it through its first couple of years is a much safer bet than one that has just opened.

scenes.purpose: Five years: the coin toss.

visual.description: Back to the cohort chart from sc12, extended to March 2020; the March 2020 bar lands at 50.2 and a faint 50% guide line appears beside it on 'coin toss'.

scenes.narration: Now the five-year mark, the one Barry's Economics used: by March 2020, 50.2 percent of the class was still operating. That is the coin toss, almost exactly.

scenes.purpose: The full decade: most do close eventually.

visual.description: The cohort chart completes to March 2025, ending at 34.7; the count line '235,071 of 677,876' appears on s28, the 'gone' line on s29.

chart.title: Class of 2015, share still operating
chart.note: All new private-sector establishments, not online stores.

onScreenText: 235,071 of 677,876 still operating
65.3% gone within the decade

scenes.narration: And ten years on, in March 2025, 235,071 were left out of the original 677,876: 34.7 percent. Put the other way, 65.3 percent were gone within the decade.

scenes.purpose: Turn from the data back to the slogans.

scenes.narration: So let's go back to the versions of the slogan we started with.

scenes.narration: The specific one, from Barry's Economics, is close on the shape: the table has about half closed within five years, though the first-year loss in this cohort is 20.4 percent rather than 25.

scenes.narration: Shopify's figure is for establishments started in 2013, and the class of 2015 we have been following also ends its decade at 34.7 percent.

scenes.purpose: Score the dramatic version against the first-year figure, with the online-store caveat on screen.

scenes.narration: And the dramatic version, nearly 90 percent gone within months, is nowhere in this table, though the table covers all new establishments, not online stores: after a full year, 79.6 percent of them were still open.

scenes.purpose: Define what the table counts: establishments, not firms.

visual.description: The BLS QCEW definition paragraph; the establishment-versus-firm sentence highlights as the narration reaches 'a firm may consist of one or more of them'.

excerpt.highlight: An establishment is in contrast to a firm, or a company, which is a business and may consist of one or more establishments

scenes.narration: So most of the new establishments in this table do close eventually, but most of them are still standing after a few years. And an establishment, in the BLS definition, is typically a single location, like a store or a factory, while a firm may consist of one or more of them.

citations.label: Jon Taylor, The Case against MLM (citing SBA and NFIB)

scenes.narration: A second set of numbers, quoted second-hand, agrees that most close eventually. Jon Taylor, in a book-length critique of multi-level marketing called The Case against MLM, cites the Small Business Administration as finding that 44 percent of small businesses survive at least four years and 31 percent at least seven. He also cites a survey by the National Federation of Independent Business in which 64.2 percent of businesses had failed over a 10-year period.

scenes.purpose: Set the SBA figures beside the class of 2015 at the same ages, with the caveat.

visual.description: Four bars in two pairs: SBA four years against the class of 2015 at March 2019, SBA seven years against March 2022. SBA bars amber, BLS bars slate.

chart.title: Survival at four and seven years
chart.note: Different agencies, years and definitions: not a like-for-like comparison.

scenes.narration: Different agencies, different years, different definitions, and the passage does not tell us exactly how either one counted. And the SBA figures Taylor cites show lower survival: 44 and 31 percent at four and seven years, against 55.4 and 43.6 percent for the class of 2015.

scenes.purpose: Signal the limits section.

scenes.narration: Before you take that curve home, there are limits to what the table can say.

scenes.purpose: Show the BLS definition of a closing in its own words.

scenes.narration: The first is what a closure means. In the BLS definition, a closing is an establishment that reported employment at the end of one quarter and none in the next.

closing

scenes.narration: That records only that the jobs at one location stopped, not why. And because survival is measured location by location, a chain that shuts one branch has a closing in this count, even if the company carries on.

scenes.purpose: Show that a sale is linked, not counted as a closing.

visual.description: The BLS FAQ answer on linking establishments over time; 'a change in ownership' highlights.

citations.label: BLS Business Employment Dynamics FAQ: linking establishments

scenes.narration: A sale is different. When an establishment changes owners, the BLS links the old record to the new one, so a sale is meant to show up as the same establishment carrying on, not as a closing.

scenes.purpose: Draw the conclusion on closures, and name the open question.

visual.description: Two lines: the first in off-white, the open question in amber.
onScreenText: Not every closure is a failure
A shop that moves address: unknown

scenes.narration: So reading every closure as a failure goes further than these definitions allow. And one question stays open: nothing in the evidence here says whether a shop that moves to a new address counts as a closing.

scenes.purpose: The second limit: no online-store breakdown anywhere in the evidence.

visual.description: Two lines built one per sentence.
onScreenText: The BLS table: no breakdown for online stores
Taylor's figures: nothing on online stores

scenes.narration: The second is the part of the slogan most of these videos care about: the table has no breakdown for online stores at all. Taylor's figures are general small-business numbers too, with nothing on online stores.

scenes.purpose: Land the verdict on the online-store claim: unchecked.

visual.description: Title appears on 'unchecked, not confirmed' and holds.
onScreenText: Unchecked, not confirmed

scenes.narration: Whether online stores close faster than a bakery or a plumbing firm is a reasonable guess, but it is a guess. The evidence here cannot tell you how long the typical online store lasts, so the claims about e-commerce stores dying within weeks or months remain unchecked, not confirmed.

scenes.purpose: Turn to the viewer's own decision.

visual.description: Question types on.
onScreenText: Thinking about starting something?

scenes.narration: So what should you do with this, if you are thinking about starting something?

scenes.purpose: Two practical takeaways from the base rate.

visual.description: Three lines built one per sentence; the third ('first year') in amber.
onScreenText: A roughly even chance of still operating after five years
Sobering, not a reason to dismiss every idea
The riskiest year is the first

scenes.narration: First, the honest base rate for a new establishment is not almost certain failure; in this cohort it was a roughly even chance of still operating after five years. That is sobering, but it is not a reason to dismiss every idea out of hand. Second, the riskiest single year is the first, when roughly a fifth of these establishments closed; planning to get through it is not a detail.

scenes.purpose: Give the viewer the questions to ask a friend and a course seller.

visual.description: Two lines built one per sentence.
onScreenText: Where does that number come from, and what does it count?
The same unchecked number, now doing a sales job

scenes.narration: Say a friend tells you almost every online store dies within months, so why bother. You can ask them where that number comes from, and what it counts. And say a course seller tells you the same thing, then offers to put you among the lucky few. That is the same unchecked number, now doing a sales job.

scenes.purpose: Replace the slogan with a better question.

visual.description: Question types on, centred.
onScreenText: What does the survival curve look like for businesses like mine?

scenes.narration: In both cases, a more useful question is: what does the survival curve look like for businesses like mine, and how will I know early if mine is on the wrong side of it?

scenes.purpose: Answer the title question with the curve's key points.

visual.description: The cohort chart returns in its sc15 colours, reduced to three bars: the start, five years, ten years.
onScreenText: 65.3% gone by ten years

scenes.narration: So, do most new businesses really fail within a few years? Not in the government's count of new establishments: about half of the class of 2015 was still operating after five years, and a clear majority, 65.3 percent, had gone by ten.

scenes.purpose: The three-part verdict on the slogan.

visual.description: Three verdict lines, each appearing as the narration reaches it: the first in slate, the second in amber, the third in grey.
onScreenText: Most, eventually: right
Most within a few years: not in this count
Most online stores within months: unchecked

scenes.narration: Most, eventually: in the government's establishment count, that part is right. Most within a few years: in that count it is not, because most were still open after three years, though the Small Business Administration figures Taylor cites, with 56 percent gone within four years, come closer to the slogan. And most online stores within months is a claim this evidence cannot check.

scenes.purpose: Close on the one thing to remember.

visual.description: Title, centred; 'curve' in slate, 'slogan' in amber.
onScreenText: Ask for the curve, not the slogan.

scenes.narration: The next time someone quotes the failure statistic at you, to scare you off or to sell you something, ask for the curve, not the slogan.
